10257.title: Impulse
10257.heading: Impulse
10257.content:
Impulse is the time integral of force and equals the change in [[Linear Momentum]]:

$$J=\int F\,dt=\Delta p.$$

For constant force, $J=F\Delta t$. On a force-time graph, impulse is the signed area under the curve. Extending the interaction time reduces the average force needed for the same momentum change.

10260.heading: Imported Geometry Unit Check
10260.content:
An imported geometry unit check compares known lengths, areas, or volumes in the receiving application with authoritative source dimensions. It detects scale factors introduced when CAD and simulation tools interpret the same coordinates under different unit systems.

The check should be a required post-import checkpoint even for simple geometry. A scale error may not produce a solver warning, yet it changes material volume, mesh size, heat-transfer area, stiffness, and every dimensional result derived from the model.

10263.title: Improper Fraction
10263.heading: Improper Fraction
10263.content:
An improper fraction is a [[Fraction]] whose [[Numerator]] is at least as large as its positive [[Denominator]]. Its value is at least one, such as (9/2).

An improper fraction may be rewritten as a mixed number, so (9/2=4+1/2). Algebra usually favors the improper form because it behaves as one quotient under multiplication, division, and symbolic manipulation. A mixed form can make size intuitive, while the improper form makes operations and cancellation more direct.

10266.title: Importance Sampling
10266.heading: Importance Sampling
10266.content:
Importance sampling draws candidates from a convenient proposal distribution and weights them by the ratio between target and proposal probabilities. The weights correct for sampling from the wrong distribution.

A proposal close to the important regions of the target yields stable estimates. A poor proposal produces a few dominant weights and wastes most samples, reducing the effective information in the computation.

An implicit function return uses the value of the last evaluated expression as the function's result. This idiom can keep short R functions concise.

For longer functions or multiple exit paths, an explicit return may communicate intent more clearly.

10272.heading: Implicit Domain Concept
10272.content: An implicit domain concept is a rule, role, distinction, or operation that participants rely on without naming clearly. Early conversations are especially vulnerable because developers fill gaps with assumptions while experts omit facts that feel obvious to them. Making the concept explicit adds it to the [[Ubiquitous Language]] and gives it a visible place in the model. Precise verbs are as important as nouns because behavior often reveals distinctions that a data glossary misses.

10275.title: Implicit Challenge
10275.heading: Implicit Challenge
10275.content:
An implicit challenge is not announced directly but must be inferred from rules, observation, experimentation, or the relationship among explicit goals. It can emerge from the system rather than being authored as a discrete objective.

Implicit challenges reward understanding, but they become unfair when essential information cannot be discovered. Feedback must let players recognize the pattern and learn from unsuccessful attempts.

10278.heading: Immutable Collections in .NET
10278.content:
An immutable .NET collection cannot change its members after construction. An operation such as adding a value returns a new collection and leaves the original instance unchanged.

This behavior makes shared data easier to reason about because one consumer cannot silently modify the version another is reading. It is particularly useful for cached or multithreaded state, though producing successive versions may cost more than mutating a private ordinary collection.

10281.title: Immune Rejection
10281.heading: Immune Rejection
10281.content:
Immune rejection occurs when a recipient's immune system recognizes an implanted tissue or its materials as foreign and attacks them. Donor-cell identity, matrix chemistry, contaminants, and degradation products can all contribute.

Using autologous cells can lower risk, but a construct's complete biological and synthetic composition must be evaluated rather than assuming the cells alone determine compatibility.

An immortalized cell line can proliferate indefinitely under suitable laboratory conditions because it acquired or was given changes that bypass normal limits on division. It supplies a consistent and expandable experimental material.

The same changes that make the line convenient can distinguish it from native donor tissue, so results must be interpreted within the model's limitations.

10287.title: Imaginary Unit
10287.heading: Imaginary Unit
10287.content:
The imaginary unit $i$ is defined by $i^2=-1$. Its powers repeat in a four-step cycle: $i, -1, -i, 1$.

It supplies the second coordinate of a [[Complex Number]]. A number $a+bi$ is real when its coefficient of $i$ is zero and purely imaginary when its real part is zero.

It is the vertical coordinate in the complex plane. The imaginary part itself is a real number, not the term $bi$.

Image-based lighting uses captured images of the surrounding illumination as the light environment for rendering virtual objects. The directional color and intensity stored in that representation produce reflections and shading related to the physical scene.

A light probe or reconstructed environment map supplies the observations. The capture must be registered to the scene, and its angular and intensity range must be sufficient for the material effects being simulated.

10296.sourceSearchName: image tampering evidence image tampering evidence
10296.title: Image Tampering Evidence
10296.heading: Image Tampering Evidence
10296.content:
Image tampering evidence is an observable inconsistency that an expected capture or encoding process does not explain. Examples include incompatible shadows, a locally missing sensor pattern, a second compression history, duplicated image structure, or metadata that conflicts with the visible scene.

Some findings directly localize an edit, while others show only that a file was resaved or passed through unexpected software. The conclusion should preserve that distinction: evidence of post-processing is not automatically evidence that the depicted event was fabricated.

10297.title: Image Tampering Evidence

10299.title: Image Resampling
10299.heading: Image Resampling
10299.content:
Image resampling creates pixel values on a new sampling grid when an image or region is scaled, rotated, stretched, or otherwise geometrically transformed. Because transformed grid locations rarely coincide with original pixels, the operation estimates new values from nearby samples.

This interpolation introduces statistical relationships that natural camera sampling does not ordinarily create. Detecting those correlations can locate a manipulated region, though ordinary resizing of the whole photograph can produce the same class of trace without deceptive editing.

10302.title: Image Recognition
10302.heading: Image Recognition
10302.content:
Image recognition is the computational task of identifying patterns or classes represented in digital images. A grayscale image can be supplied to a neural network as a [[Matrix]] of pixel-intensity values, with each value serving as an input feature.

During [[Supervised Learning]], labeled images form a training dataset and a separate test dataset measures generalization. A multiclass output layer can assign probabilities to possible object categories through a [[Softmax Function]].

10304.title: Image Provenance
10304.heading: Document
10304.content:
2026-09-16 00:47

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Image Authenticity and Forensic Reasoning]]

10305.title: Image Provenance
10305.heading: Image Provenance
10305.content:
Image provenance is the history connecting a digital photograph to its source, capture device, and subsequent transformations. [[Reverse Image Search]] can expose earlier appearances or altered variants, while [[EXIF Metadata]], JPEG signatures, and sensor traces can supply evidence about the device or software involved.

No single trace normally reconstructs the entire history. Metadata can be removed, search indexes are incomplete, and a file can be repeatedly transcoded. A provenance judgment is strongest when independent content, format, and capture clues converge on the same account.

10307.sourceSearchName: image of group homomorphism image of group homomorphism
10307.title: Image of Group Homomorphism
10307.heading: Document

10308.sourceSearchName: image of group homomorphism image of group homomorphism
10308.title: Image of Group Homomorphism
10308.heading: Image of Group Homomorphism
10308.content:
The image of a group homomorphism is the set of target elements attained by the map. It forms a subgroup of the target.

The first isomorphism theorem identifies this image with the source modulo the kernel.

10309.title: Image of Group Homomorphism

10310.title: Image Metadata

10311.title: Image Metadata
10311.heading: Image Metadata
10311.content:
Image metadata are descriptive records stored alongside pixel data. They may identify the camera make and model, lens and exposure settings, capture time, geographic coordinates, editing software, copyright information, and an embedded preview.

Metadata support forensic reasoning when fields agree with one another and with the visible photograph. They are not intrinsically trustworthy: software can edit or remove them, online services often strip them, and a forger can copy plausible values from another file. Their evidentiary value lies in specific consistencies and contradictions.

10314.sourceSearchName: image formation pipeline image formation pipeline
10314.title: Image Formation Pipeline
10314.heading: Image Formation Pipeline
10314.content:
The image formation pipeline begins with the scene and its illumination, continues through camera optics and a light-sensitive sensor, and ends with in-camera processing and file encoding. Each stage imposes physical, geometric, or statistical regularities on the resulting pixels.

[[Digital Image Forensics]] works backward through this pipeline. A composite may preserve plausible objects while disrupting their shared light, perspective, interpolation correlations, sensor noise, or JPEG history. Modeling the stages separately helps an analyst choose evidence that is relevant to the suspected alteration.

10315.title: Image Formation Pipeline

10317.sourceSearchName: image forensics countermeasure image forensics countermeasure
10317.title: Image Forensics Countermeasure
10317.heading: Image Forensics Countermeasure
10317.content:
An image forensics countermeasure is a manipulation intended to erase, imitate, or avoid a detector's expected trace. A skilled forger can alter metadata, reinsert noise, equalize compression, or adapt generated imagery after learning how a forensic method works.

This creates a continuing contest between authentication and fabrication. New methods expose regularities that current tools overlook, while new forgeries are designed around published tests. The possibility of countermeasures is why a clean result should not be treated as conclusive proof of authenticity.

10318.sourceSearchName: image forensics countermeasure image forensics countermeasure
10318.title: Image Forensics Countermeasure
10318.heading: References

10319.title: Image Authenticity
10319.heading: Document

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Image Authenticity and Forensic Reasoning]]

10320.title: Image Authenticity
10320.heading: Image Authenticity
10320.content:
Image authenticity is the claim that a photograph represents an unaltered output of its stated capture process. Forensic examination cannot prove this claim absolutely: a clean result means only that the applied techniques did not find evidence of tampering under their operating conditions.

Negative findings carry different weight for different files. A high-resolution image with intact metadata and strong physical cues is more testable than a compressed, downsampled, or stripped copy. Authentication is therefore an evidence-weighting judgment, not a binary property supplied by one tool.

10322.sourceSearchName: ill posed learning problem ill posed learning problem
10322.title: Ill-Posed Learning Problem

10323.sourceSearchName: ill posed learning problem ill posed learning problem
10323.title: Ill-Posed Learning Problem
10323.heading: Ill-Posed Learning Problem
10323.content:
Function learning is ill posed when the available examples do not determine one unique mapping from inputs to outputs. Kelleher illustrates this with several candidate arithmetic rules: more than one rule can match the observed examples, even though they disagree on unseen inputs.

Noise and a large space of possible functions make the problem harder. More examples may distinguish candidates, but collecting them can be expensive or impossible. A [[Machine Learning]] algorithm therefore combines evidence from a [[Training Dataset]] with an [[Inductive Bias in Machine Learning|inductive bias]] that favors some candidate functions. The bias makes learning possible without proving that the favored function is the one true explanation.

10326.title: Ill-Conditioned Linear System
10326.heading: Ill-Conditioned Linear System
10326.content:
An ill-conditioned linear system is one whose solution changes greatly under small changes in coefficients or the right-hand side. Its [[Matrix Condition Number]] is large.

Ill-conditioning is a property of the problem, not simply of the chosen algorithm. Pivoting, stable factorizations, and [[Iterative Refinement]] can reduce additional numerical damage but cannot remove the underlying sensitivity.

10329.title: IdentityServer
10329.heading: IdentityServer
10329.content:
IdentityServer is middleware that adds OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.0 endpoints to an ASP.NET Core application. It connects the application's identity records to clients that need tokens and standardized authentication flows.

An SPA profile defines defaults such as login and logout callback locations, allowed response types, and scopes. Development signing settings should remain environment-specific rather than being copied into production configuration.

The stock-checker project presents IdentityServer 4 as a framework for running an identity service rather than a prebuilt external provider. Its configuration identifies users, protected API resources, and clients, then supplies signing credentials so issued tokens can be trusted by the API.

10332.title: IEEE 802.11b
10332.heading: IEEE 802.11b
10332.content:
IEEE 802.11b was an early widely adopted wireless networking standard. It specified interoperable radio communication for local-area networks and helped move Wi-Fi from ad hoc products into mainstream devices.

Standardization let equipment from different vendors connect through common access points. Intel’s integration of Wi-Fi into laptop chipsets further accelerated adoption.

10335.sourceSearchName: identity server signing credential identity server signing credential
10335.title: IdentityServer Signing Credential
10335.heading: IdentityServer Signing Credential
10335.content:
An IdentityServer signing credential signs issued tokens so a protected API can verify that they came from the trusted authorization server and were not altered. A development credential is convenient for local setup but is not the intended production identity of the server.

The project replaces its temporary credential with a certificate selected from the Windows certificate store by thumbprint. Key deployment and trust must be planned separately from application code; a self-signed demonstration certificate is not presented as production assurance.

10336.title: IdentityServer Signing Credential

10338.title: Identity Theft
10338.heading: Identity Theft
10338.content:
Identity theft is the unauthorized use of information associated with another person to impersonate them or obtain benefits. User-generated platforms expose names, locations, relationships, routines, and preferences that can be combined into convincing fraudulent profiles.

Protection involves minimizing unnecessary disclosure, detecting abnormal account behavior, strengthening authentication, and preventing sensitive attributes from being inferred from public context.

10341.title: Identity Matrix
10341.heading: Identity Matrix
10341.content:
The identity matrix is a [[Square Matrix]] with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. It is the multiplicative identity: $IA=AI=A$ whenever the dimensions are compatible.

It appears in the definitions of a [[Matrix Inverse]] and the [[Characteristic Equation]]. Subtracting $\lambda I$ from a matrix shifts its diagonal entries when forming an eigenvalue problem.

10343.sourceSearchName: identifier versus predictive attribute identifier versus predictive attribute
10343.title: Identifier versus Predictive Attribute

10343.content:
2026-09-15 09:05

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Data Science Framing and Representation]]

10344.sourceSearchName: identifier versus predictive attribute identifier versus predictive attribute
10344.title: Identifier versus Predictive Attribute
10344.heading: Identifier versus Predictive Attribute
10344.content:
An identifier labels an instance so its records can be joined, checked, or traced. Although it may occupy a column in an analytic table, the identifier is generally not a substantive predictor of the target. Treating arbitrary ID values as meaningful features can invite accidental patterns.

The distinction belongs to data understanding: a column's machine-readable type does not reveal its analytical role. A number can be an ID, a count, an ordered rating, or a measured quantity, and those roles permit different transformations and interpretations.

10345.sourceSearchName: identifier versus predictive attribute identifier versus predictive attribute
10345.title: Identifier versus Predictive Attribute
10345.heading: References

10347.title: Identity Element
10347.heading: Identity Element
10347.content:
An identity element leaves every value unchanged under a particular operation. Zero is the additive identity because

$$a+0=0+a=a,$$

and one is the multiplicative identity because

$$a\cdot1=1\cdot a=a.$$

Identity is operation-specific: zero does not act as the multiplicative identity, and one does not act as the additive identity. These elements support inverse operations. An [[Opposite Number]] combines with its original through addition to reach zero, while a [[Reciprocal]] combines through multiplication to reach one.

10350.title: Identifier Exclusion
10350.heading: Identifier Exclusion
10350.content:
Identifier exclusion removes record keys and near-unique labels from model inputs while retaining them for joins and auditing. Identifiers can let a flexible learner memorize training cases without discovering a transferable relationship.

The field remains valuable operationally, so exclusion from a formula should not mean deletion from the governed dataset.

10352.title: Ideal
10352.heading: Document

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Ring and Ideal Foundations]] · [[Quotient Rings and Ideals]]

10353.title: Ideal
10353.heading: Ideal
10353.content:
An ideal I in a [[Commutative Ring]] is closed under subtraction and under multiplication by arbitrary ring elements. The ideal generated by a collection consists of all finite ring-linear combinations of its generators.

Ideals are precisely the kernels available to [[Ring Homomorphism]]s and the substructures by which [[Quotient Ring]]s are formed. Prime, maximal, radical, primary, and finitely generated ideals capture different structural properties.

The source motivates ideals by asking when multiplication of additive cosets is well defined. Closure under multiplication by every ring element is exactly the condition that makes the coset product independent of representatives.

10355.title: Ideal Quotient
10355.heading: Document
10355.content:

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Prime Ideals and Noetherian Algebra]]

10356.title: Ideal Quotient
10356.heading: Ideal Quotient
10356.content:
For ideals I and J in a ring R, the ideal quotient (I:J) consists of elements r such that rJ is contained in I. It measures which multipliers force all of J into I.

The special case (0:J) is the annihilator of J. Replacing J by successive powers produces the [[Saturation of an Ideal]], which collects elements that enter I after multiplication by a sufficiently high power.

10365.content:
The ideal gas equation combines the empirical gas laws:

$$pV=nRT=Nk_BT.$$

Pressure $p$, volume $V$, absolute temperature $T$, and amount of gas are linked through the molar gas constant $R$ or Boltzmann constant $k_B$. Real gases approach ideal behavior at low density and sufficiently high temperature.

10371.title: ID3 Algorithm
10371.heading: ID3 Algorithm
10371.content:
ID3 recursively constructs a decision tree from categorical training data. If all examples at a node share a class it creates a leaf; otherwise it chooses the best remaining feature, branches on its values, distributes the examples, and repeats.

The best feature is selected through information gain. Basic ID3 does not directly handle numeric attributes, missing values, or noise without extensions.

10374.content:
IBM introduced its Personal Computer in 1981 using an Intel processor and components supplied largely by outside vendors. The company’s reputation helped the machine enter businesses rapidly.

Its relatively open component structure and externally supplied operating system made it easier for competitors to build compatible machines. The resulting ecosystem shifted industry power away from IBM.

IBM PC compatible clones reproduced the interfaces and behavior needed to run software written for IBM’s machine. Standard processors and third-party components made hardware imitation easier than in earlier mainframes.

Compatibility expanded consumer choice and drove prices down, while reinforcing MS-DOS as the common platform. IBM could not maintain exclusive control over the architecture it popularized.

IBM initially marketed it as a defense calculator, reflecting the government funding behind early demand. Its success helped move the dominant punched-card supplier into electronic computing.

10386.content:
Hypothesis-driven regression fits a model to evaluate a relationship specified before the outcome analysis. The exposure and outcome remain central, while candidate covariates are included to address plausible confounding rather than to maximize prediction alone.

At least one representation of the exposure stays in every model iteration so the final model can answer the hypothesis. If its adjusted estimate is not statistically or substantively meaningful, the appropriate conclusion is that the data do not support the proposed relationship.

Hypothesis-driven development states what the team believes a change will cause, for whom, and within what constraint, then builds the smallest test that can challenge the belief. A useful hypothesis connects an intervention to an observable result.

10392.title: Hypertext
10392.heading: Hypertext
10392.content:
Hypertext is text containing references that connect one part of a document to another document or location. These references are [[Hyperlink|hyperlinks]] that a reader can follow while navigating related information.

On the web, linked documents collectively form a [[Web Graph]]. The link structure is not merely navigational; [[PageRank]] interprets it as evidence about which pages other authors considered important enough to reference.

10395.title: HyperMap Embedding
10395.heading: HyperMap Embedding
10395.content:
HyperMap embeds a scale-free network in the [[Poincare Disk Model]] by approximately maximizing the likelihood of its observed links. It orders nodes by degree, associates that order with arrival time, assigns radial coordinates, and estimates angular coordinates from local likelihoods.

Unlike distance-preserving embedding, HyperMap tries to reconstruct a plausible hyperbolic growth process. The inferred coordinates can also predict missing links because nearby non-neighbors receive a higher connection probability.

10398.title: Hyperparameter
10398.heading: Hyperparameter
10398.content:
A hyperparameter is a modeling choice set outside the ordinary parameter-fitting step. The neighbor count in [[K-Nearest Neighbors]], the span in LOESS, and the number of retained dimensions are examples that control flexibility or representation.

Choosing the value by minimizing training error creates optimistic bias. [[Cross-Validation]] estimates performance on held-out folds so competing hyperparameters can be compared without using the final test set for tuning.

Kelleher contrasts manually fixed neural-network choices with weights fitted during training. The selected [[Activation Function|activation function]], [[Convolutional Stride|convolution stride]], and [[Learning Rate|learning rate]] are examples of choices that shape the training procedure or architecture rather than being adjusted by the ordinary parameter update.

The book tunes decision-tree complexity and loss choices by comparing held-out behavior, and it controls ensemble capacity through settings such as feature sampling, tree count, depth, learning rate, and boosting rounds. These choices shape the fitted procedure without being ordinary learned coefficients.

10401.title: Hypernetwork
10401.heading: Hypernetwork
10401.content:
A hypernetwork generalizes an ordinary graph by allowing one hyperlink to connect more than two nodes. The network is defined by a node set and a family of nonempty node subsets that serve as its hyperlinks.

This representation is useful when a relationship belongs to a group as a whole rather than decomposing naturally into independent pairs. Pairwise projection can lose that joint structure.

10404.title: Hyperlink
10404.heading: Hyperlink
10404.content:
A hyperlink is a reference from text to another location in the same document or to a different document. On the web, a hyperlink creates a directed connection from its source page to its destination page.

These connections turn pages into a [[Web Graph]]. Incoming links become [[Backlink|backlinks]], and PageRank treats each outgoing link as receiving part of the source page's relative importance.

10406.title: Hyperlink Matrix

10407.title: Hyperlink Matrix
10407.heading: Hyperlink Matrix
10407.content:
A hyperlink matrix normalizes an [[Adjacency Matrix]] by dividing each nonzero entry in a row by the number of outgoing links represented in that row. Every linked destination thereby receives an equal share of the source page's importance.

Multiplying the [[PageRank Vector]] by this matrix redistributes rank through the [[Web Graph]]. Rows of zeros created by pages with no outgoing links require correction before the [[Power Method]] can produce a reliable ranking.

10410.title: Hypergraph Partitioning
10410.heading: Hypergraph Partitioning
10410.content:
A hypergraph edge can connect more than two vertices, preserving multiway relationships that an ordinary graph would decompose into pairwise links. Hypergraph partitioning divides vertices while minimizing cut hyperedges under balance constraints.

This representation is useful for transactions, circuits, and relational data in which one event joins many objects. The cut definition must specify whether splitting a hyperedge once or across several blocks carries different cost.

10413.title: Hyperbolic Space
10413.heading: Hyperbolic Space
10413.content:
Hyperbolic space is a non-Euclidean metric space with negative curvature. In two dimensions, the circumference and area available at a given radius grow exponentially rather than at the polynomial rate of Euclidean space.

That expansion resembles the growth of nodes with distance from the root of a tree. It makes hyperbolic space a useful latent geometry for representing hierarchical and scale-free [[Graph|networks]].

10416.title: Hyperboloid Model
10416.heading: Hyperboloid Model
10416.content:
The hyperboloid model realizes hyperbolic space as one sheet of a hyperboloid embedded in a higher-dimensional real space. A specialized inner-product relationship defines distances between points on that surface.

The model is useful for coordinate computation and underlies the [[Rigel Embedding]] method. Perspective projection can transform it into the [[Poincare Disk Model]] without changing the represented geometry.

10419.sourceSearchName: hyperbolic radial fin geometry hyperbolic radial fin geometry
10419.title: Hyperbolic Radial Fin Geometry
10419.heading: Hyperbolic Radial Fin Geometry
10419.content:
A hyperbolic radial fin varies its thickness along a profile defined by a hyperbolic relationship and extends around a central axis. The profile can be parameterized in a work plane and revolved to create the three-dimensional solid.

The changing thickness redistributes material between the base and outer radius. Profile continuity, minimum thickness, volume, and surface measurements are necessary checks before comparing the design with constant-thickness radial fins.

10422.sourceSearchName: hyperbolic network visualization hyperbolic network visualization
10422.title: Hyperbolic Network Visualization
10422.heading: Hyperbolic Network Visualization
10422.content:
Hyperbolic network visualization places a large hierarchy or graph in a finite view whose available space expands rapidly away from the center. Moving a region toward the center enlarges its detail while compressing distant context toward the boundary.

The technique can show global hierarchy, centrality, and community structure while retaining local neighborhoods. The geometric transformation supports an adaptive focus instead of permanently discarding off-center nodes.

10425.sourceSearchName: hyperbolic network embedding hyperbolic network embedding
10425.title: Hyperbolic Network Embedding
10425.heading: Hyperbolic Network Embedding
10425.content:
A hyperbolic network embedding assigns coordinates in [[Hyperbolic Space]] to graph nodes. One approach approximates observed graph distances, while another chooses coordinates that make the observed network likely under a hyperbolic growth model.

Once embedded, coordinate distance can accelerate shortest-path estimates, centrality calculations, missing-link prediction, routing, and visualization. The value of the embedding depends on both its computational cost and its structural distortion.

10428.title: Hyperbolic Distance
10428.heading: Hyperbolic Distance
10428.content:
Hyperbolic distance measures separation under a negatively curved geometry rather than ordinary Euclidean distance. Its formula depends on the chosen coordinate model, but isometries preserve the same underlying distance relationships.

For embedded networks, one distance can combine a node's radial popularity and angular similarity. Thresholding the distance can infer correlations or links, while comparing it to graph distance evaluates an embedding's distortion.

10430.sourceSearchName: hyperbolic greedy routing hyperbolic greedy routing

10430.heading: Document

10431.sourceSearchName: hyperbolic greedy routing hyperbolic greedy routing
10431.title: Hyperbolic Greedy Routing
10431.heading: Hyperbolic Greedy Routing
10431.content:
Hyperbolic greedy routing forwards a message to the neighbor whose coordinate is closest in [[Hyperbolic Distance]] to the destination. Each node needs only its neighbors' coordinates and the destination coordinate rather than a global routing table.

The method is highly successful in networks whose topology fits a hidden hyperbolic geometry, and its routes can approach shortest paths. It fails at a local minimum when no neighbor is closer, unless the embedding or forwarding rule supplies a recovery mechanism.

10434.sourceSearchName: hyperbolic dimensionality reduction hyperbolic dimensionality reduction
10434.title: Hyperbolic Dimensionality Reduction
10434.heading: Hyperbolic Dimensionality Reduction
10434.content:
Hyperbolic dimensionality reduction maps high-dimensional points into a lower-dimensional [[Hyperbolic Space]] while controlling distance distortion. Reducing to two or three dimensions can make the same coordinates useful for analysis and visualization.

Landmark methods and randomized transforms reduce the cost of processing large datasets. The technique is especially suited to hierarchical data because low-dimensional hyperbolic space can preserve tree-like expansion more naturally than a flat plane.

10437.heading: Hyperbolic Data Correlation

Hyperbolic data correlation represents data items as coordinates and treats sufficiently small [[Hyperbolic Distance]] as evidence of a relationship. A distance threshold controls how far each inferred neighborhood extends.

Latent features can be assigned to radial and angular coordinates before links are created. This produces a network representation that can feed clustering, embedding, navigation, link prediction, and visualization within the same geometric framework.

10440.title: Hydrostatic Pressure
10440.heading: Hydrostatic Pressure
10440.content: Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure increase caused by the weight of fluid above a point. For a uniform fluid of density $\rho$ in a uniform gravitational field, the excess pressure at depth $h$ is $\Delta p=\rho gh$. It depends on depth and density rather than the vessel's shape.

10443.heading: Hydrogen-Oxygen Fuel Cell
10443.content: A hydrogen-oxygen [[Fuel Cell]] combines hydrogen with oxygen to produce water and electrical work. Hydrogen loses electrons at one electrode, and the external circuit carries them to the oxygen-side reaction; ions move through the [[Fuel Cell Electrolyte]] to maintain charge balance. For one mole of hydrogen consumed, the ideal reaction produces one mole of water. Real output is below the reversible limit because of polarization losses.

10449.title: Hydrogen Safety
10449.heading: Hydrogen Safety
10449.content: Hydrogen systems need deliberate leak, ignition, flame, pressure-surge, and explosion controls because hydrogen-air mixtures can ignite over a wide range and the flame can be difficult to see. The source lists pressure-rated equipment, relief provisions, flame traps, and rapid closing as design concerns. This note describes the book's engineering principles, not a current safety code or complete operating procedure.

Transport therefore is not cost-free merely because hydrogen is a light gas. It connects production sites to storage and end users within a larger [[Hydrogen as Energy Carrier]] system.

A hydrogel is a water-rich polymer network whose soft mechanical behavior can resemble biological tissue. Cells can be embedded while the material is liquid and retained when physical, thermal, chemical, or light-driven crosslinking turns it into a gel.

Natural hydrogels carry biological signals; synthetic hydrogels offer tighter control over stiffness, chemistry, and degradation.

A hybrid random walk moves within user or item domains and across user-item links in a star-structured graph. Steady-state probabilities estimate user tie strength, item relevance, and the likelihood of adoption or rejection.

Updates combine routes through similar users, similar items, labels, and observed cross-domain behaviors. This transfers auxiliary knowledge into a target recommendation while addressing [[Behavioral Data Sparsity]] and the [[Cold-Start Problem]].

10476.title: Hybrid Pricing
10476.heading: Hybrid Pricing
10476.content:
Hybrid pricing combines two or more pricing mechanisms in one cloud-service agreement. A subscription may include volume tiers, or a fixed monthly amount may permit usage within agreed limits while an outcome component rewards additional value.

Combining models can balance predictable spending, affordability, risk transfer, and incentives. It also makes comparison harder, so each component's measurement, thresholds, and contractual term should remain explicit.

The architecture responds to different cost and latency needs rather than declaring one storage system universally superior. Its usefulness depends on whether data meaning, access rights, query execution, and result integration remain coherent across the two places.

The components normally need to share data, processes, or control. A hybrid design can keep sensitive work in a [[Private Cloud]] while using standard public services for flexibility, or can duplicate a service in another cloud for continuity and [[Cloud Bursting]].

10488.title: Humanism in AI
10488.heading: Humanism in AI
10488.content:
Humanism in AI places human reason, dignity, freedom, or flourishing at the center of judgments about intelligent technology. It rejects the idea that technical capability or efficiency should determine its own goals and insists that machines should serve human purposes.

The position protects people from being subordinated to automated systems, but it can treat a historically specific picture of the human as universal. It may also neglect nonhuman life and environmental interests. [[Posthumanism]] and [[Anthropocentrism in AI Ethics]] expose these limits without eliminating the practical need to defend people against concentrated technological power.

10491.title: Human-Robot Empathy
10491.heading: Human-Robot Empathy
10491.content:
Human-robot empathy is the tendency to respond to a robot's apparent vulnerability, emotion, or social behavior as if the robot could be helped or harmed. Appearance, movement, voice, and interaction can make even a simple machine feel like a social participant.

Empathy does not demonstrate [[Machine Sentience]], but it has ethical consequences. Mistreating a robot can distress people, shape habits, and alter expectations about social conduct. Designers can also exploit empathy to secure trust or compliance. This makes emotional presentation part of the ethical design of a [[Social Robot]], not merely an aesthetic feature.

10494.title: Human-Machine Symbiosis
10494.heading: Human-Machine Symbiosis
10494.content:
Human-machine symbiosis envisions computers as partners that extend human cognition rather than replacements that automate people away. J. C. R. Licklider promoted interactive systems in which machines handle storage and calculation while people guide goals and interpretation.

The idea requires rapid feedback and direct access. It motivated time-sharing, graphical interaction, and networking research that moved computing beyond isolated batch jobs.
